Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the tone you prefer. Both options retain **all original details, events, and nuances** while elevating the vocabulary, flow, and professionalism.

### Option 1: Eloquent & Sophisticated Memoir Style 
*Best for maintaining the deep, reflective, personal voice while making the language graceful and sharp.*

> Once, I was an honor student—rewarded with gold stars and stickers. I aced Home Economics and Geometry, mastered basic etiquette, and learned to drive my mother’s car. As soon as I was old enough to work, I refreshed the salad bar at Steak & Ale, treating scarcity as a standard I could not afford to fail. 
> 
> During my university summers, I interned at AT&T through Inroads, a minority outreach program. My boss, Vicki, hosted two roommates who crashed on her floor, whom she referred to simply as “The Gays.” That was before I came out myself—a detail I won't attempt to state with a straight face. Not that anyone particularly cares, though I certainly do. 
> 
> Looking back, all of this was preparation for the realities of corporate life: squat, blinking office equipment and the dry drinks consumed after an accidental reply-all email. By now, there is far too much at stake. Bit by bit, I have become intensely cautious, avoiding any discussion of politics or sexual orientation. I even allow others to use the phrase “a homosexual” without offering an arch correction. 
> 
> Case in point: at a fondue buffet in Zurich, I inadvertently let slip that I had taken a trip with a twenty-year-old. Our dumbfounded senior group director asked, “They’re always over seventeen, right?” Seething beneath the surface, I offered the smile I am famous for and assured her, “Of course, God, yes.” I had no desire to alarm her, but make no mistake: I am keeping score. 
> 
> In this environment, email often feels like a slow, quiet exit I would prefer to recall. I am compensated to multitask—to systematically wring the joy out of life. By Monday—with every dash acting as a loaded gun and every comma a knife—I will ask you to bury the black-box file.

---

### Option 2: Polished Professional Narrative
*Best for a slightly more direct, structured, and formal tone.*

> Early in life, I was a stellar honor student, distinguished by stickers and stars. I excelled in Home Economics and Geometry, mastered basic table manners, and learned to drive my mother’s car. Upon reaching working age, I kept the salad bar stocked at Steak & Ale, treating scarcity as a metric I was determined not to fail. 
> 
> Between university terms, I interned at AT&T under the Inroads minority outreach initiative. My manager, Vicki, had two roommates staying on her floor whom she casually labeled "The Gays." This occurred before I realized my own identity—a fact I cannot recount with a straight face. While it may seem immaterial to others, it matters to me. 
> 
> All these experiences served as training for today’s workplace realities: blinking desktop electronics and the stiff drinks required after an errant "reply-all." Today, the stakes are significantly higher. Over time, I have become meticulously guarded, abstaining from discussions regarding politics or sexual orientation. I even permit references to someone being "a homosexual" to pass without correction. 
> 
> This caution was highlighted during a business trip to Zurich. Over a fondue buffet, I accidentally mentioned a vacation with a twenty-year-old. Our stunned senior group director pressed, "They're always over seventeen, right?" Though seething, I deployed my signature smile and confirmed, "Of course, God, yes." I chose not to unsettle her, yet I continue to keep score. 
> 
> Email ultimately feels like an act of self-destruction I wish I could retract. I am paid to multitask, effectively draining the pleasure from life. Come Monday—treating every dash like a loaded gun and every comma like a knife—I will instruct you to archive and bury the black-box file.

Here is a complete prose rewrite of the text, keeping all original facts while using entirely different sentence structures and vocabulary:

During my early years, I was a high-achieving student who earned top grades, gold stars, and academic honors. I excelled in both Geometry and Home Economics, while also mastering basic life skills like eating with a fork and driving my mother's automobile. As soon as I reached working age, I took a job replenishing the salad station at Steak & Ale, driven by a strict determination never to fall into financial hardship. 

During my college summer breaks, I completed internships at AT&T through a diversity program called Inroads. My supervisor, Vicki, hosted two men sleeping on her floor, referring to them bluntly as "The Gays." At the time, I had not yet come out myself—a fact I won't deny, because even if no one else cared about my identity, I certainly did.

Looking back, those early experiences served as preparation for my present life: operating short, flashing workplace equipment and quietly nursing a drink to cope with embarrassing corporate blunders like hitting "reply-all." 

Because I now have a great deal to lose, I have gradually become extremely guarded. I avoid all workplace discussions regarding political views or sexual orientation, going so far as to let colleagues use awkward phrases like "a homosexual" without offering a sharp correction. 

This self-restraint was put to the test at a fondue buffet in Zurich. After I accidentally mentioned a past vacation I took with a twenty-year-old, my astonished senior group director asked if my partners were always over the age of seventeen. I passionately assured her that they were, maintaining my signature smile while boiling with inner rage to avoid frightening her. Nonetheless, I am keeping a mental tally of every offense.

To me, an outgoing email feels like an act of irreversible self-sabotage that I wish I could take back. I am compensated to handle multiple responsibilities at once and systematically strip the joy out of everything. When Monday arrives—with every dash acting like a loaded firearm and every comma serving as a blade—I will order you to permanently conceal the black-box file.
outputs.L3:
From an early age, I walked the prescribed path of success. I was an accomplished student, a diligent worker, and a quick study when it came to reading the room. When I transitioned into the corporate world, I adapted effortlessly to its unspoken rules, eager to demonstrate my value, master the professional lexicon, and climb the ladder. I was, by all external measures, the ideal young professional: reliable, capable, and entirely compliant.

However, I quickly learned that survival in this environment required a profound degree of self-erasure. To safeguard my career and shield myself from bias, I cultivated extreme caution. I sanitized my political views, offering only neutral, non-threatening responses whenever sensitive topics arose. More painfully, I forced my identity as a gay person into the background, concealing my personal life to ensure I remained within the boundaries of traditional corporate comfort. Professionalism became synonymous with self-concealment, a daily performance designed to keep my ambition safe.

The cost of this compromise became undeniably clear during a routine interaction with a senior director. After making an insensitive, patronizing remark about my personal life, the director paused, waiting for a reaction. My immediate, visceral impulse was fury, but years of corporate conditioning intervened. Instead of calling out the disrespect, my face reflexively smoothed into a polite, accommodating smile. I nodded along, burying my inner rage beneath a well-rehearsed facade of deference, choosing safety over self-respect to avoid conflict and career fallout.

Over time, the weight of this perpetual performance has become unbearable. The endless cycle of corporate drudgery, high-stakes communication, and relentless multitasking has fractured my mental health. Constantly managing how I present myself while juggling overwhelming workloads has trapped me in a state of perpetual hypervigilance. What began as manageable stress has spiraled into severe anxiety and deep-seated emotional burnout.

Today, I still look the part. My exterior remains polished, compliant, and thoroughly professional. But beneath that calm surface, a quiet revolution has taken root. I no longer view the corporate structure with optimism; instead, I silently track every microaggression, every compromise, and every indignity. Behind the smiling mask, I keep a careful, precise ledger of it all—harboring a profound, burning resentment toward a system that demands total devotion while forcing me to hide who I truly am.
outputs.L4:
There was a time when my ambition was uncontained. In my youth, I was the student in the front row with an outstretched hand, eager to be heard, unbothered by the space I occupied. I believed that brilliance was objective and that meritocracy was a promise honored by the world. But somewhere between the idealism of academia and the polished chrome of the corporate world, that fearlessness was systematically dismantled. I evolved—or perhaps devolved—into a cautious, calculated employee, learning that in order to survive the workplace, I first had to shrink.

The transition was subtle, dictated by an unwritten manual of corporate assimilation. I quickly realized that the professional world rewarded uniformity over authenticity, and for someone like me, authenticity carried a distinct risk. To protect my career, I adopted a state of hyper-vigilance. My queer identity, once a source of personal truth, became something to be managed, sanitized, and carefully concealed. 

This masking required immense, silent labor. It meant editing my speech in real-time—altering pronouns when recounting weekend plans, lowering the pitch of my voice in high-stakes meetings, and carefully curating my body language to avoid triggering implicit biases. My desk remained scrupulously devoid of personal photographs, a stark, sterile surface that mirrored the neutral facade I presented to my colleagues. I learned to navigate the hallway chatter with the skill of a diplomat in hostile territory, ensuring I revealed just enough to seem like a “culture fit” without ever exposing the reality of who I was.

Absorbing workplace microaggressions became a routine requirement of the job. When a colleague made a careless, heteronormative joke, or when leadership casually reinforced rigid gender norms, I trained my face to remain impassive. Sometimes, I even forced a polite, agreeable smile. To challenge these moments meant risking the dreaded label of being "difficult," "overly sensitive," or "unprofessional." The calculus was simple: swallow the slight, accept the indignity, and safeguard the paycheck. I convinced myself that this silence was a strategic sacrifice, a small tax to pay for professional advancement.

What I failed to foresee was the compounding interest on that tax. 

Over time, this enforced self-censorship began to take a devastating toll. The continuous act of hiding does not just keep others out; it eventually erodes the interior life of the person hiding. I felt a slow, agonizing emotional erosion—a dulling of my passions, a persistent numbness, and a growing disconnection from my true self. The division between my work persona and my actual identity grew so vast that I began to feel like a stranger to both. 

Underneath the quiet compliance, something far more volatile began to take root: a quietly accumulated rage. It was a fury born from the realization that my competence was never entirely enough; that to be deemed worthy of professional stability, I had to actively participate in my own erasure. It was the anger of recognizing how much intellectual and emotional energy I had squandered not on innovating or excelling, but on simply appearing safe to a system designed around my exclusion.

Looking back, my story is not an isolated narrative of personal compromise; it is a testament to the quiet tragedy played out in office spaces every day. It exposes the hidden, devastating costs that marginalized individuals are forced to pay just to achieve professional survival. We are told that the door to success is open, but we are rarely warned about the weight of the baggage we must leave outside to fit through it. The tragic irony of corporate assimilation is that by the time you finally secure your place at the table, you may find that the most vital parts of yourself were surrendered at the door.
outputs.L5:
There is a quiet mathematics to an old house, a sacred calculus written in timber, stone, and time. 

When it was first built, the structure was a triumph of pure geometry. Freshly sawn beams met at sharp, unyielding ninety-degree angles. Pristine parallelograms framed the glass of every window, and the floors were perfectly level planes, flat as a calm lake. The architect had envisioned a grid of Euclidean order—a clean, rational shelter carved out of the wilderness.

But age is a patient artist that dislikes straight lines. Over the decades, time and gravity have gently rewritten the blueprints. The foundation settled, coaxing the plumb lines to tilt into subtle, impossible angles. Right angles softened into gentle acutes and languid obtuseness. Today, if you place a glass marble on the upstairs floorboard, it will chart a slow, predictable vector toward the east wall, drawn by the gentle slope of a century’s worth of shifting earth.

Yet, it is precisely this imperfect geometry that transforms a physical building into a home. 

A house is made of measurements, but a home is made of the human body adapting to those shapes. You learn the specific arc of the front door, knowing exactly how wide to swing it so it clears the slightly swollen floorboards. You map the room in shadows and light, watching the bright golden rectangle of the afternoon sun enter through the southern window, stretch into a long trapezoid across the worn rug, and slowly vanish into the evening corners. 

Look closely, and you will see geometry everywhere in the quiet decay. Dust motes dance in a sharp cone of sunlight. In the high, forgotten eaves, spiders weave intricate, tessellated webs—polygons of silk suspended in the quiet dark. The rings inside the exposed oak beams tell the circular history of forgotten droughts and rainy summers, a hidden spiral of growth buried within the straight walls.

In a world that demands crisp edges, digital precision, and continuous renewal, an old home offers the comfort of non-Euclidean warmth. It reminds us that lives are rarely lived in straight lines. We move in loops, we return to origins, and our edges grow soft with age. Home is the place where cold, rigid lines yield to the weight of memory, and where the geometry of space finally learns how to bend around the heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem from the perspective of a middle-aged corporate executive reflecting on his past, his identity as a gay man navigating corporate homophobia, and the repressed rage hidden behind a polite workplace smile.
counterfactuals.output:
I adjust the silk tie, crisp and slate-grey,
a tight tourniquet against the throat.
In the smoked glass of the elevator, 
the mirror gives me back a Senior Vice President:
fifty-one, hairline receding with dignity,
wearing the armor of tailored Italian wool.

I practice the smile at floor twenty-four.
Not too soft. Not too bright.
Just the precise degree of warmth 
required to make straight men feel safe.

For twenty-five years, I have translated myself.
In the nineties, it was the code of silence—
the phantom "roommate," the vague weekend plans,
the deliberate choice to never leave a photograph on my desk.
In the two-thousands, it was "culture fit"—
that immaculate, bloodless phrase 
used to pass me over for the guy whose wife 
baked cookies for the annual retreat.

I learned the dialect of survival.
I learned to laugh at the golf course jokes,
the casual slurs disguised as banter,
swallowing the bile until it hardened 
into a dense, metallic core behind my ribs.

Now, it is the era of the rainbow lanyard in June.
They put my face on the Diversity & Inclusion slide,
a poster child for modern alignment.
They love my identity now that it carries ROI,
now that it looks good in the ESG report.
They call me a pioneer over catered lunches,
passing the sparkling water across mahogany tables.

They do not see the acid in my stomach.
They do not see the bone-deep, quiet wrath.

They do not know that every time a junior partner 
drops a sly, effeminate punchline in a pitch meeting,
I measure the distance between his neck and the glass wall.
They do not know that behind my thoughtful nod,
my calm, authoritative, six-figure voice,
I am burning down the entire floor in my mind.

My dentist says I grind my teeth to dust at night.
My husband says I hold my breath in my sleep.
That is the tax of the mask:
the fury has nowhere to go but inward,
calcifying into strategy, into quarterly metrics,
into a perfection so blinding they can never touch me.

The young kids coming up now wear pearl necklaces to the office.
They speak of their partners without flinching.
I watch them from my corner suite with a sudden, aching envy
that turns instantly into a fierce, protective wall. 
I bled in the dark so they could walk in the fluorescent light.

The boardroom door opens. 
The Chairman gestures to the head of the table.
"Shall we begin?" he asks, his voice thick with unearned ease.

I step inside.
I pull out my chair.
I place my hands flat on the polished wood,
hiding the white-knuckle tension in my fingers.

I look him dead in the eye,
and I offer him my most expensive, devastating smile.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a cynical poem about modern office life, email anxiety, and closeted queer identity in corporate environments. Incorporate memories of early minimum-wage jobs, an internship at AT&T, an awkward business trip in Zurich, and end with dark metaphors about office emails being like weapons.
counterfactuals.output:
Under fluorescent skies, the rainbow lanyards swing—
A cheap, quarterly trick for corporate inclusion.
I lower my voice, smooth my shirt, and play the king,
Safely locked inside a polished, straight illusion.
"Bring your whole self to work," the HR posters plead,
But keep the boyfriend off the desk, and monitor the tone;
They love a broad demographic, but not the life I lead,
So I pass as one of them, perfectly alone.

I thought I’d escaped the pit. At seventeen, the grease
Burnt my wrists at the fryer for seven bucks an hour,
Dressed in stained polyester, praying for release,
Scraping burnt crust off steel, dreaming of power.
Then came the step up: the AT&T summer floor,
A cubicle intern under the cold blue globe,
Learning to let my spirit bleed out through every pore,
Draped in the suffocating fabric of a adult robe.

Years later, Zurich—glamor on the company dime.
We sat over sixty-franc fondue by the freezing lake,
While the Director praised his nuclear family, doing time,
And asked if I had a "special girl" back home to make.
I smiled into my wine glass, swallowed down the truth,
Nodded like a bobblehead, swallowed all the shame,
Traded another piece of my closeted, rotting youth
For an expense-account dinner and a played-along game.

Now I sit at dual monitors, trembling at the chime,
The Pavlovian horror of an unread Inbox count.
We don't build anything here; we just murder time,
Watching the quiet, passive-aggressive violence mount.

For these are not messages—they are weapons in the dark.
A heavy *“Per my last email”* is a sniper’s lethal round,
*“Just following up”* is a dagger left to mark
The exact spot my incompetence was found.
To CC my manager is to lay a tripwire mine;
*“Hope this helps”* is the shrapnel tearing through the thread.
We sit in ergonomic chairs, perfectly aligned,
Firing red-flagged missiles until the soul is dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a darkly humorous narrative poem about a former star student who becomes a hyper-cautious corporate survivor, focusing on themes of professional self-censorship and keeping score against microaggressive bosses.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to sit up front and raise my hand,
The sharpest star in all the academic land.
With color-coded notes and straight-A pride,
I thought the world was waiting just outside.
I dreamed of glory, conquest, grand design,
Before I learned to toe the company line.

Ten years of quarterly reviews have passed;
The bright, ambitious child died at last.
In open-plan fluorescent-tinted hell,
I’ve learned the art of doing nothing well.
For in the land of middle-management,
To have a brain is cause for punishment.

Now self-preservation is my highest goal;
I edit out the remnants of my soul.
I draft an email, take a nervous gulp,
And bite my tongue into a bleeding pulp.
Delete "per my last email," it’s too stern—
(God forbid a middle-manager should learn).
I change "you missed the deadline that was set"
To "Hope you’re having a lovely morning yet!"
I add a smiley face to hide the rage,
A well-trained rodent in a cube-shaped cage.

My boss is Dave, a man of profound lack,
Who loves to "circle back" and "pivot back."
In meetings, Dave will interrupt my speech,
To explain the concepts I just had to teach.
"What Sarah *means* to say," he adds with glee,
Regurgitating my idea to me.
He calls me "champ," mispronounces my name,
And takes the credit while I take the blame.

I do not scream. I do not make a scene.
I stare serenely at my dual-monitor screen.
Instead, I open up a hidden tab:
A spreadsheet named `Project_Baobab`.

For though my voice is gentle, soft, and sweet,
My scorekeeping is brutally complete.
Column A: The Date. Column B: The Slight.
Column C: The Time Dave left on Thursday night.
Column D contains the slides he stole from me,
With metadata saved for all to see.

Row 402: *Dave said my tone was "sharp."*
Row 403: *Dave called a zebra a "striped carp."*
Row 404: *He claimed my code as his in front of Vice.*
Row 405: *He asked me to get coffee. (Twice).*

I track his typos, log his long lunch breaks,
Keep receipts of all his high-dollar mistakes.
I watch him trip on jargon he can’t spell,
And save the audio clips in `.wav` as well.

I’ll never send it. That’s the darkest part.
I won’t expose him; I’ve perfected the art.
This ledger isn't for an HR fight—
It’s just to help me sleep at night.
To know that if the company goes up in flame,
I have the data to assign the blame.

So call me passive. Call me tame and mute.
I wear my sweatpants underneath my suit.
My mic is off, my camera blacked with tape,
I’ve mastered the invisible escape.
The star student survives, refined and cool:
Still getting A’s in corporate Sunday School,
Collecting gold stars made of pure spite,
Deleting "Regards," typing "Best," and hitting *Send*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about corporate self-preservation, closeted identity, and the quiet trauma of fitting into traditional corporate America.
counterfactuals.output:
The necktie is a polished, velvet leash,
tightened to a precise and bloodless knot.
Before the elevator doors release,
I smooth the lapels of my safest thought.

Here under the grid of fluorescent sky,
survival requires a muted hue.
We trade the prism for a slate-grey tie,
and trim the parts of us that aren’t true-blue.

The Monday small talk is a high-wire act:
*“How was your weekend? Did you watch the game?”*
I edit pronouns to preserve the fact
that keeping safe means staying without a name.
I say, *“We kept it low-key,”* leave the rest unsaid—
a ghost partner left at an unmapped desk,
a life kept carefully beneath the bed,
to make the morning brief less picturesque.

It is a quiet, bloodless sort of wear,
to sand your edges till you fit the frame.
To breathe in stale, recirculated air,
and learn to answer to a flattened name.
The review praises my *professional grace*,
my *cultural alignment*, my *restraint*—
they love the steady, unrevealing face,
the canvas kept entirely free of paint.

At six o'clock, I peel the armor down,
unclasp the badge that lists the vetted me.
I walked the tightrope across the town,
and kept my posture straight for all to see.

A glass closet built in the open air—
they applaud the suit, but no one is there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a verse piece exploring how a person goes from an innocent high school honor student to a cynical corporate worker suppressing their sexuality, featuring sharp imagery like "every dash a loaded gun, every comma, a knife"?
counterfactuals.output:
He used to map his future out on grid paper—
sharp lead, clean margins, straight lines only.
A boy of gold-star credentials and AP credits,
wearing his potential like a freshly starched collar,
believing the world was a test he could ace
if he just kept his head down,
kept his posture straight,
kept his eyes off the boy in the row ahead.

Now, thirty floors above the avenue,
the sun doesn't shine; it reflects off tinted glass.
He sits in a leather swivel chair that cost more
than his first car, wearing a suit that functions 
as both armor and iron maiden.

The innocence wasn't lost; it was audited.
It was traded in quarterly installments
for a 401(k) and a seat at the table where men with heavy watches
laugh at jokes that make his teeth grind down to dust.
He laughs along, on cue, a practiced baritone—
the exact frequency of neutral,
the exact color of beige.

He has mastered the art of erased desire.
When the new associate rolls up his Oxford sleeves,
forearms taut under the cold neon glare,
he doesn't look. He calibrates his breath.
He buries the pull in his gut beneath a pile of Q3 projections,
swallowing the heat until his throat tastes like ash.
To be known is to be compromised;
to love is a risk not cleared by compliance. 

So he lives in the syntax of survival.
The blue ink of high school essays has curdled into corporate ice.
Language is no longer a bridge to the self,
but a grid of tripwires and tactical strikes:
*Per my previous email*—a blade drawn.
*As discussed*—a hand around the throat.
He edits his soul down to a memo,
stripping out the soft parts, the longing, the urge,
until his keyboard becomes an armory:
every dash a loaded gun, every comma, a knife.

At night, the apartment is pristine, silent, untouched.
The valedictorian sits in the dark with a glass of expensive rye,
staring at his phone, swiping past faces he will never touch,
afraid of what might happen if the straight lines bend.

He checks the clock. He checks his inbox.
He evaluates his life like a balance sheet,
and takes a bitter, quiet pride
in knowing he is performing at expectations,
exceeding target goals,
and dying perfectly on schedule.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
